planting.note: Sow seed on a sandy, nutrient-poor peat mix kept constantly wet with rain or distilled water in full sun and high heat; like its better-known relative B. liniflora, this tropical northern-Australian species is grown as a fast warm-season annual bog plant.

directions: A slender Australian sundew relative with wiry, thread-like leaves densely covered in sticky glandular hairs that passively trap small insects, the mucilage catching light in tiny rainbow glints that give the genus its common name. Small five-petaled mauve to purple flowers open along the upper stems through the warm growing season. It shares the same lean, wet, sunny culture as other annual rainbow plants: a sandy, mineral-poor peat mix kept permanently saturated with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, since tap water minerals quickly stunt and kill it. Being a true annual, it completes its life cycle in a single season and self-sows readily if a few flowers are allowed to set seed, which can be collected and resown the following spring once the weather is reliably warm.

planting.note: Plant the bulb horizontally with the crown near the substrate surface in nutrient-rich aquarium substrate; deep burial invites bulb rot before roots establish.

directions: A bulb-forming Madagascan aquatic grown fully submersed as a fast-growing aquarium centerpiece, prized for its large, translucent, ruffled-edge strap leaves in a lighter yellow-green than most other sword-leaved Aponogeton. It tolerates lower light than many stem plants but grows noticeably larger and faster under medium to strong light with root tab fertilizer near the bulb; CO2 injection speeds growth but is not required. Its flower spike is distinctively forked into two branches once it reaches the surface, unlike the single unbranched spike of the similar Aponogeton crispus, and self-pollinates readily to set viable seed. After a flowering cycle the bulb often enters a brief rest with reduced leaf production before resuming growth; avoid disturbing it during this period.
sources: Tropica Aquarium Plants — Aponogeton ulvaceus species profile

planting.note: Root stem cuttings lightly in nutrient-rich substrate under moderate to strong light fully submersed in an aquarium, or at a warm, frost-free pond margin as an emersed marginal.

directions: A South American stem plant grown fully submersed in freshwater aquaria, forming bushy clusters of small, bright green, oval leaves along slender branching stems that create a soft, airy mid-ground or background mass. Under moderate to strong light it branches freely from every leaf node, filling in quickly, while under weak light it stretches thin and sparse with widely spaced leaves. It roots easily from cut stem sections pushed into the substrate and tolerates a wide range of water chemistry, making it a forgiving, fast-filling choice for new aquarium plantings. Given very bright light it can also produce small white, star-shaped flowers when allowed to grow emersed above the waterline at a pond or paludarium margin, the trait behind its common name.
sources: Tropica Aquarium Plants — Heteranthera zosterifolia species profile
University of Florida IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

planting.note: Plant small rosette divisions into fine, nutrient-rich substrate fully submersed under strong light with supplemental CO2; this species is far more demanding than the hardy native pipeworts and sulks without stable, soft, slightly acidic water.

directions: A diminutive tropical Asian wetland herb grown fully submersed in planted aquascapes, forming tight, symmetrical rosettes of narrow, grass-like leaves prized by aquascaping hobbyists for the fine, star-shaped texture it adds to a foreground or mid-ground carpet. Unlike the coarser native pipeworts grown as pond-margin bog plants, this miniature species is a demanding specialist that needs strong light, injected CO2, soft and slightly acidic water, and a nutrient-rich substrate to thrive, and it is prone to melting away if any of those conditions lapse. It multiplies slowly by producing small plantlets at the base of mature rosettes, which can be separated and replanted once they have their own roots. Because of its exacting needs it is grown almost exclusively as a specialist aquarium plant rather than as an outdoor pond or bog plant.
sources: Tropica Aquarium Plants — Eriocaulon cinereum species profile

planting.note: Set rhizomes with the crown at or just below the substrate surface in loose, mineral-rich mix at the shaded margin of a warm-climate pond or bog filter; elsewhere grow fully submersed in an aquarium or emersed in a paludarium and overwinter indoors.

directions: A Southeast Asian rhizomatous aroid grown equally well fully submersed in an aquarium, emersed at a shaded pond margin in frost-free climates, or in a humid paludarium, forming low clumps of narrow, lance-shaped leaves with distinctly undulating, wavy margins in olive-green to coppery-brown tones. It tolerates lower light than many other Cryptocoryne species, making it a dependable foreground or mid-ground plant for dimmer tanks, though like its relatives it can shed its leaves in a temporary die-back known as 'crypt melt' when moved or when water chemistry shifts abruptly, recovering from the rhizome within a few weeks. Divide the slowly spreading rhizome mats every year or two to propagate and control spread, and keep it above the mid-60s Fahrenheit year-round, since it has no cold tolerance outside the tropics.
sources: Tropica Aquarium Plants — Cryptocoryne undulata species profile
